title: Smartphones Replacing Personal Computers
source_note: Based on the officially confirmed 2025 Paper 4 version 1.3, “As PC ownership declines, smartphones are on the rise”. Passage and questions are original.

context.source_line: This article appeared on a youth / education website:
context.title: One Device for Everything?
body: For many young people, the smartphone is their camera, map, wallet, television and main way of going online. It is cheaper and more portable than a laptop, and most everyday tasks—messaging, shopping, banking and watching videos—can be completed with a few taps. As phones become more powerful, some families no longer see a reason to own a separate computer.

Nevertheless, a small screen is not ideal for every task. Writing a long report, analysing a spreadsheet, editing a video or comparing several sources is usually easier with a full keyboard and a larger display. Relying only on phones may also create an educational gap: students can consume information easily but struggle to produce complex work. Instead of asking which device will completely replace the other, consumers should consider which tool is appropriate for each task and whether shared computers can provide affordable access.

body: Introduction to Beekeeping can be viewed from several angles: personal experience, public interest and the practical limits of putting an idea into action. People's relationships with animals can support conservation, education, companionship and well-being. Direct experience may build interest and empathy when it is managed responsibly.

For Introduction to Beekeeping, these possible benefits need to be weighed carefully. Human enjoyment must not come before an animal's welfare or the protection of its natural environment. title: Digital Museums
source_note: Based on the officially confirmed 2024 Paper 4 version 1.1, “Digital museum”. Passage and questions are original.

context.source_line: This article appeared on a youth / education website:
context.title: Can a Museum Fit Inside a Phone?
body: Digital museums allow visitors to explore high-resolution images, 3D models and recorded stories without travelling. A student can rotate an ancient object on screen, zoom in on details that are difficult to see behind glass and revisit an exhibition after class. Digital access also helps people who live far away or have mobility difficulties.

But a virtual tour cannot reproduce the size, texture and atmosphere of a real object in a physical space. Some users click quickly from one image to another without reading deeply. Museums also face costs: items must be photographed, described, translated and stored securely. A better approach may be to connect the two experiences. An online preview can build curiosity before a visit, while interactive maps and audio guides can enrich the visit itself. The goal should not be to replace museums, but to make their collections more accessible and meaningful.

body: Debate about Unattractive Buildings in Hong Kong shows how one idea can create opportunities for some people while raising practical concerns for others. Movement and the design of public space influence where people can work, study and spend their free time. Improvements may increase access, safety and the attractiveness of a neighbourhood or destination.

For Unattractive Buildings in Hong Kong, these possible benefits need to be weighed carefully. Major changes can also disrupt residents, increase costs or favour visitors over local needs. A balanced plan should examine safety, accessibility, environmental impact and the experience of the people who use the place every day.

body: Interest in The Cross-Harbour Race has encouraged people to compare familiar approaches with newer possibilities. The best choice may depend on purpose, audience and circumstances. Movement and the design of public space influence where people can work, study and spend their free time. Improvements may increase access, safety and the attractiveness of a neighbourhood or destination.

For The Cross-Harbour Race, these possible benefits need to be weighed carefully. Major changes can also disrupt residents, increase costs or favour visitors over local needs. title: Wearable Smart Devices
source_note: Based on the officially confirmed 2023 Paper 4 version 4.1, “Wearable smart devices”. Passage and questions are original.

context.source_line: This article appeared on a youth / education website:
context.title: When Your Watch Knows More About You Than You Do
body: Smartwatches, rings and sensor-equipped clothing can count steps, measure heart rate and estimate sleep quality. Some devices remind users to move after long periods of sitting, while others can send an alert when they detect an unusual pattern. For athletes and patients, continuous data may reveal changes that a short clinic visit cannot capture.

However, wearable data is not always accurate or easy to interpret. A low sleep score may create anxiety even when the user feels well. Personal information may also be stored by technology companies, shared with other services or exposed in a data breach. In schools, wearables create another problem: a smartwatch can receive messages and may be used unfairly during tests. title: Screen-time Controls for Teenagers
source_note: Based on the officially confirmed 2019 topic title “Apple Screen Control”. Passage and questions are original.

context.source_line: This article appeared on a youth / education website:
context.title: Can a Phone Teach Us When to Put It Down?
body: Most smartphones now include tools that show users how much time they spend on different apps. They can also block selected apps after a daily limit, silence notifications during study time and provide weekly reports. Supporters say these tools turn an invisible habit into something measurable. A teenager who thinks she uses social media for only an hour may be surprised to discover that the real figure is three hours.

However, limits do not automatically create self-control. Users can often press an ‘ignore’ button, change the settings or move to another device. Strict controls set by parents may also damage trust and encourage secretive behaviour. Some psychologists therefore recommend a family agreement instead: everyone, including adults, keeps phones away during meals and before bedtime. title: Translation Apps and Language Learning
source_note: Based on the officially confirmed 2019 topic title “Translation Apps”. Passage and questions are original.

context.source_line: This article appeared on a youth / education website:
context.title: A Helpful Language Partner — or a Dangerous Shortcut?
body: Translation apps have become fast, cheap and easy to use. A traveller can point a phone camera at a menu, while a student can listen to the pronunciation of an unfamiliar phrase. The apps can reduce anxiety and help people communicate in emergencies. They are particularly useful when users need the general meaning of a message rather than a perfect translation.

Yet a smooth translation may still be misleading. Apps can miss humour, cultural references and the speaker’s tone. Students who paste entire assignments into a translator may submit unnatural sentences without understanding the grammar. Teachers also worry that constant dependence prevents learners from thinking directly in the target language. Used carefully, an app can act like a dictionary, a pronunciation guide and a checking tool. Used carelessly, it becomes a shortcut that hides mistakes instead of correcting them.

context.source_line: Adapted practice article based on the 2012 HKDSE Paper 4 Set 8.2 topic:
context.title: Thinking Carefully about Plastic Surgery for Men
body: People may first see Plastic Surgery for Men as a straightforward topic, yet its effects depend on who takes part, what resources are available and how success is judged. Environmental proposals ask people to think beyond immediate convenience and consider effects on shared resources, animals and future communities. Local action can also make a large issue feel more manageable.

For Plastic Surgery for Men, these possible benefits need to be weighed carefully. Good intentions are not enough if a scheme simply shifts waste, cost or inconvenience elsewhere. Measures may fail when the public cannot understand them or when greener choices are difficult to afford. For this reason, examples should be examined carefully rather than treated as proof that the same approach will work for everyone.

The group can organise its ideas around “What kinds of men would seek plastic surgery”, before moving to “The reasons for its increasing popularity” and “Any negative aspects of plastic surgery”. A workable plan needs clear responsibilities, realistic incentives and a way to measure its environmental benefit over time.

context.title: Memory Training: What Should Be Considered?
body: Memory Training can be viewed from several angles: personal experience, public interest and the practical limits of putting an idea into action. The topic involves choices that may offer clear benefits to some people while changing expectations for others. Personal experience can help explain a view, but it does not represent every situation.

For Memory Training, these possible benefits need to be weighed carefully. An attractive idea may carry hidden costs, practical limits or unintended effects. Different stakeholders may also use different standards when deciding what counts as success. Any recommendation should be realistic enough to carry out and flexible enough to respond when circumstances change.

The group can organise its ideas around “The benefits of training one's memory”, before moving to “How one's memorizing ability can be trained” and “The types of people who could benefit from having an improved memory”. A balanced decision should compare alternatives, identify who is affected and support each recommendation with relevant reasons and examples.
